findings.title: Stored XSS: a resource's attacker-chosen mimetype is used verbatim as the Content-Type of an inline file download on the CKAN origin
findings.evidence: ckan/views/resource.py:175-181 serves an uploaded resource with `resp = flask.send_file(filepath)` (inline; no as_attachment, no Content-Disposition: attachment) and then overrides the type with the resource's own field: `if rsc.get(u'mimetype'): resp.headers[u'Content-Type'] = rsc[u'mimetype']`. The mimetype field is caller-supplied and unconstrained: ckan/logic/schema.py:48 declares `'mimetype': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe]` - no allowlist, no pattern. ckan/logic/action/create.py:307-309 and ckan/logic/action/update.py:292-294 only fill mimetype in when the caller omitted it (`if 'mimetype' not in data_dict`), so a caller-supplied 'text/html' survives to the database. The stored bytes are unconstrained too: verify_type() exists only on ckan/lib/uploader.py:200-236 (the Upload class used for group/user/admin images) and has no counterpart on ResourceUpload, so resource uploads are never type-checked. Route: ckan/views/resource.py:949 and :954 register `/<resource_id>/download` and `/<resource_id>/download/<filename>` under the dataset blueprint. A tree-wide grep for `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Frame-Options` across ckan/ and ckanext/ returns zero matches, so nothing downstream blunts it. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no layer between the field and the header - the assignment at line 179-180 is the last transformation); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (value traced back to the `mimetype` key of a resource_create/resource_update call); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the sink is a real HTTP Content-Type on a document the browser renders); FP-04 DOES_NOT_HOLD (core view, no flag); FP-10 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no CSP exists to bound it).
findings.impact: Any principal who can create a dataset and attach a resource - on a default CKAN this includes any self-registered user - uploads a file containing HTML and JavaScript and sets its mimetype to text/html. Every visitor who opens the download URL executes that script on the CKAN origin. The auth_tkt cookie is HttpOnly by default (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:95), so this is not direct cookie theft, but the script can drive the whole /api/3/action surface as the victim: change the victim's email and trigger a password reset, add itself as a collaborator, or - if the victim is a sysadmin - promote the attacker. The same field also lets an attacker serve application/pdf, image/svg+xml or text/html for arbitrary bytes, which turns the portal into a hosting origin for phishing pages under the operator's domain.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the resource `mimetype` validator in ckan/logic/schema.py to a small allowlist of non-active types, or ignore the stored value entirely when serving and derive the Content-Type server-side. Independently, serve uploaded resources with `Content-Disposition: attachment` (flask.send_file(..., as_attachment=True)) and add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every response in ckan/views/__init__.py's after-request pipeline. The strongest fix is to serve user-uploaded files from a separate origin so that a Content-Type mistake cannot reach the session.

findings.title: Log injection (CWE-117): the unauthenticated password-reset form field is written into a line-oriented log without neutralisation
findings.evidence: ckan/views/user.py:610 binds `id = request.form.get(u'user')` and line 616 writes it straight into the log: `log.info(u'Password reset requested for user "{}"'.format(id))`. The same value reaches a second sink at lines 650-651: `log.info(u'User requested reset link for unknown user: {}'.format(id))`. No escaper, validator or pattern sits between the bind and either sink - the value is used raw before any user lookup happens. The endpoint is anonymous: ckan/views/user.py:862-863 registers `/reset` for RequestResetView, and its only gate is `logic.check_access(u'request_reset', ...)` (line 604), whose auth function is ckan/logic/auth/get.py:409-410 `def request_reset(context, data_dict): return {'success': True}`. The consumer is line-oriented by construction: ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:257-258 ships `[formatter_generic] format = %(asctime)s %(levelname)-5.5s [%(name)s] %(message)s` over a StreamHandler, so one CR/LF in the field produces two records. The value arrives percent-decoded through Werkzeug form parsing (werkzeug==1.0.0, requirements.txt), so `user=alice%0D%0A2026-08-25+12:00:00,000+INFO++[ckan.views.user]+Password+reset+completed+for+admin` is a single POST that writes a second, fabricated record. Note the bundled enumeration flagged both lines as UNCLEARED; reading for the pattern would not have: the two sinks are eleven lines apart and neither looks unusual. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (request.form.get, unauthenticated); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the format is line-oriented text, named above); FP-09 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-10 DOES_NOT_HOLD (this is not merely an accountability loss, the record is forgeable).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller writes arbitrary, well-formed records into the application log. Because the log is the evidence trail for account-recovery abuse, an attacker running a reset-spray can bury it: forge 'Password reset completed' lines for other accounts, forge lines attributed to other loggers, or inject a volume of plausible records that makes the real sequence unrecoverable. Where the log is shipped to an aggregator with a line parser, the forged records enter the index as genuine events and can drive alerting rules; where it is rendered in a web log viewer, an injected line carrying markup becomes stored XSS in the viewer, reached without ever authenticating to CKAN.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise control characters at the sink, not at the caller: strip or escape CR, LF and other C0 characters from any externally supplied value before it reaches a logging call - a small helper applied at every such site is the only version of this that stays fixed. Better still, move to a structured (one JSON object per event) handler so that a newline inside a field cannot become a record boundary, and confirm the consumer parses that format. Fix ckan/views/user.py:616 and :650 together; the identical pair exists in the legacy Pylons controller at ckan/controllers/user.py:482 and :486.

findings.title: Log injection (CWE-117): the unauthenticated API action name from the URL path is logged without neutralisation
findings.evidence: ckan/views/api.py:509-512 registers `/action/<logic_function>` and `/<int:ver>/action/<logic_function>` for GET and POST. When the name does not resolve, lines 256-260 do `msg = u'Action name not known: {0}'.format(logic_function)` followed by `log.info(msg)`. `logic_function` is the raw path segment. Werkzeug's default string converter is `[^/]+`, which in Python's `re` matches a newline, and PATH_INFO reaches the application percent-decoded per PEP 3333, so `GET /api/3/action/x%0A2026-08-25%20INFO%20%20[ckan]%20forged` produces a value containing a real newline. Same line-oriented formatter as above (ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:258). No authentication is required to reach this branch - the failure happens before any context or auth check is built (the context dict is only constructed at line 262). Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (URL path segment, anonymous); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-10 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: The highest-volume anonymous surface in the product doubles as a log-write primitive: one GET per forged record, no session, no rate limit in core. Same consequences as the reset-form sink - forged records, poisoned aggregator index, and stored XSS in any HTML log viewer.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise CR/LF in `logic_function` before the log call, or log a repr rather than the bare string. Applying the same shared sanitiser used for the reset-form fix is preferable to a local patch.

findings.title: Log injection (CWE-117): every request's decoded PATH_INFO is written to the log by the global after-request hook
findings.evidence: ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:423-426 reads `url = request.environ['PATH_INFO']` and logs `log.info(' %s %s render time %.3f seconds' % (status_code, url, r_time))`. PATH_INFO is the percent-decoded path (PEP 3333), so `%0A` in the request line arrives as a real newline in this variable. The hook is registered globally and runs for every response, including 404s, so no route needs to exist for the sink to fire. Contrast with the Pylons twin at ckan/lib/base.py:312-313, which logs `request.environ['CKAN_CURRENT_URL']` - that value is built at ckan/views/__init__.py:325-334 by `u'/'.join(quote(pce, u'') for pce in path_info.split(u'/'))`, which percent-re-encodes each path segment and therefore neutralises the newline. The two sites read alike; only one is safe, and it is the safe one that is written in the awkward style. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the quoting control exists in the codebase but is not on this path); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-10 DOES_NOT_HOLD.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller writes a forged record with a single request to any path, existing or not. Because the hook logs the status code alongside the path, an attacker can forge records that look like successful requests for privileged paths, which is exactly the shape a responder looks for when reconstructing an incident.
findings.recommendation: Log the already-neutralised `request.environ['CKAN_CURRENT_URL']` here as the Pylons path does, or apply the same per-segment quoting to PATH_INFO before the call. A structured handler would close it at the format level.

findings.title: Log injection (CWE-117): resource_id path parameter logged raw by the resource proxy
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:105-107 registers `/dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy`; line 33-34 does `resource_id = data_dict[u'resource_id']` then `log.info(u'Proxify resource {id}'.format(id=resource_id))`. The log call happens at line 34, before the `resource_show` lookup at line 35, so an arbitrary decoded path segment reaches the sink whether or not the resource exists. Same decoding argument and same line-oriented formatter as the two findings above. A second raw sink is at ckanext/resourceproxy/plugin.py:37. Severity is one step lower only because the plugin is not enabled by default (it must be added to ckan.plugins). Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-04 UNKNOWN - I cannot see the deployment's ckan.plugins from this tree, so this finding is reported as probable rather than confirmed, and its ceiling is set by that answer.
findings.impact: On any site running the resourceproxy plugin, an unauthenticated caller forges log records via the proxy URL. Same consequences as above, on a narrower installed base.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise the value before the call, and move the log statement after the successful `resource_show` so an unknown id cannot reach it at all.

findings.title: API key and bearer token written to the log in clear text (CWE-532)
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:260-283 collects the credential from the X-CKAN-API-Key header, then from the WSGI environ, then from HTTP_AUTHORIZATION, and at line 277 logs it whole: `log.debug(u'Received API Key: %s' % apikey)`. The value logged is the credential itself, in full - line 279 uses the same string as an equality lookup against `model.User.apikey`, and line 281 passes it to `api_token.get_user_from_token`, so it is a live bearer credential and not a derivative. Nothing redacts, truncates or hashes it. This function runs on every request that carries the header, for every user including sysadmins. I am not reproducing any value here, per the safety contract. Notable: the bundled enumeration reported this line as `cleared`, crediting the `six.ensure_text(...)` call on line 276 as if it neutralised the value; it does not - it is an encoding coercion. This is the exact failure mode web-api-logging.md warns about ('Do not read a `cleared` line as a clearance'), and I found it by reading the function rather than by trusting the column. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (no redaction filter exists anywhere in the logging configuration - ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:220-262 declares no filter); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (it is precisely the attacker-relevant secret); FP-07 DOES_NOT_HOLD (an API key is a credential, not low-value data); FP-04 DOES_NOT_HOLD - the level is DEBUG, but ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:245-247 sets the ckan logger to INFO while `[logger_root] level = WARNING`, and operators routinely raise CKAN to DEBUG to diagnose exactly the kind of auth problem that puts this line in the log; a level that production is expected to switch on is not a shipping-path exclusion.
findings.impact: Whoever can read the application log - an operator, a log-shipping pipeline, a backup, a compromised aggregator account, or an attacker who has already obtained log read access through a lesser bug - obtains live API keys and JWT bearer tokens belonging to every user who made an API call while DEBUG was on, sysadmins included. CKAN API keys do not expire, so the exposure does not age out on its own. This also converts a low-severity log-read into full account takeover, which is the usual way this class turns into a real incident.
findings.recommendation: Never log the credential. If a diagnostic marker is needed, log a fixed-length prefix or a hash - and gate it so no configuration re-enables the full value. Add a redaction filter to the shipped logging configuration for `apikey`, `Authorization`, `password` and `token`, and rotate any keys that appear in existing logs.

findings.title: SSRF: the resource proxy fetches any user-stored URL from the server's network position with no destination restriction (WEB-10)
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:38-71: `url = resource[u'url']` (a value the resource's owner writes), then the only check is `parts = urlsplit(url); if not parts.scheme or not parts.netloc: return abort(409, ...)` at lines 40-42 - a presence check, not a destination check. The URL then goes to `requests.head(url, timeout=TIMEOUT)` (line 49) and `requests.get(url, timeout=TIMEOUT, stream=True)` (lines 55 and 69). There is no allowlist, no denylist, no private/loopback/link-local address check, no DNS re-resolution after redirect, and redirects are not disabled - `requests` follows them by default, so even a check placed on the initial URL would not survive. The response body is streamed back to the caller (lines 74-82), so this is a full read-SSRF, not a blind one. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (I searched for an egress control in the repository - there is none in this extension, in ckan/config, or in the shipped Dockerfile/uwsgi config); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the URL is the user-supplied `url` field of a resource); FP-04 UNKNOWN for the same plugin-enablement reason as the log finding above, so this is probable rather than confirmed.
findings.impact: Any principal who can create a resource points it at an address only the server can reach and then reads the response through the proxy: the cloud instance metadata service on 169.254.169.254 (credentials, on an unhardened IMDSv1 host), Solr on the internal network, an internal admin panel, or a port scan of the private range inferred from response timing and status. The proxy is designed to be fetched by the browser during a preview, so the request is made with the server's identity and its network position, which is the whole point of the class.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the hostname and reject any address in a private, loopback, link-local or multicast range before connecting, and re-check after every redirect (or set allow_redirects=False and validate each hop). Restrict schemes to http and https explicitly. Where the deployment allows it, put the proxy behind an egress proxy that enforces the destination policy at the network layer, so a code path that forgets the check still cannot reach the metadata service.

findings.title: The resource proxy copies the remote server's Content-Type onto a response served from the CKAN origin
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:71 sets `response.headers[u'content-type'] = r.headers[u'content-type']` - the type is taken verbatim from the remote server the attacker chose in the resource URL - and lines 74-76 stream that remote body into the response. The route is `/dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy` on the CKAN origin (line 105-107). Nothing constrains the type to a preview-safe set, and the tree contains no `X-Content-Type-Options` or `Content-Security-Policy` header anywhere (grepped across ckan/ and ckanext/). Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD (both the URL and, through it, the response headers are attacker-chosen); FP-03 DOES_NOT_HOLD (the browser renders it as whatever the header says); FP-04 UNKNOWN (plugin enablement), so probable rather than confirmed.
findings.impact: An attacker registers a resource whose URL points at a server they control which answers `Content-Type: text/html` with a script. Any user who opens the proxy URL executes it on the CKAN origin. This is the same same-origin consequence as the resource-download finding, reached by a different route, and it defeats the reason the proxy exists - the proxy was introduced to work around the same-origin policy for previews, and it currently does so in the attacker's favour.
findings.recommendation: Map the remote type onto an allowlist of preview-safe types and fall back to application/octet-stream (or refuse) for anything else; never copy the header through. Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and serve the proxy from a separate origin.

findings.title: A successful password reset does not invalidate the user's existing sessions, and the reset key never expires
findings.evidence: ckan/views/user.py:725-750: after `user_update` sets the new password, the only cleanup is `mailer.create_reset_key(context[u'user_obj'])` at line 748, which rotates the reset key. Nothing invalidates issued auth_tkt cookies. Those cookies are self-contained tickets signed with a site-wide secret (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:85-88 falls back to `beaker.session.secret`) and carry the user *name*, not a password-derived value or a server-side session id, so a ticket minted before the reset keeps validating afterwards. Separately, the reset key has no lifetime: ckan/lib/mailer.py:205-211 stores `codecs.encode(os.urandom(16), 'hex')` into `user.reset_key`, and ckan/model/user.py:40 declares `Column('reset_key', types.UnicodeText)` with no companion timestamp column; ckan/lib/mailer.py:214-219 verifies it with `key.strip() == user.reset_key` and a length check only - no expiry, and a non-constant-time comparison. Triage: FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD (I looked for a server-side session store that a reset could clear - repoze auth_tkt has none); FP-02 DOES_NOT_HOLD; FP-10 DOES_NOT_HOLD for the session half (the whole point of a reset under compromise is to evict the attacker). The 128-bit key from os.urandom is sound, so the predictability half of WEB-03 does not apply.
findings.impact: The standard recovery action after 'I think someone is in my account' does not evict the attacker: their existing cookie keeps working until it times out on its own. Compounding it, an old reset email is a permanent credential - anyone who later reaches the victim's mailbox, an archived message, or a proxy log containing the link can take the account over at any point in the future, provided no newer reset has been requested.
findings.recommendation: Invalidate outstanding tickets on password change - the practical route with auth_tkt is to include a per-user token in the ticket userid or userdata and rotate it on reset, which makes every prior ticket fail verification. Give the reset key a stored issue time and reject it past a short window (an hour is typical). Compare it with hmac.compare_digest.

findings.title: No anti-CSRF token on state-changing forms: the helper that would emit one is a stub returning an empty string
findings.evidence: The only occurrence of the string 'csrf' in the whole Python tree is ckan/lib/helpers.py:3030-3031: `@core_helper def csrf_input(): return ''`. There is no token generation, no token store, and no verification anywhere - state-changing views read the form and act (for example ckan/views/user.py:610 and ckan/views/resource.py:187-196 with no token check). The only thing standing between a cross-site POST and the action is the cookie attribute: ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:99 sets `samesite = config.get(u'who.samesite', 'lax').lower()` and lines 61-66 emit SameSite=Lax by default, which browsers do not attach to cross-site POSTs. Triage: FP-01 HOLDS-PARTIAL, and I am recording it as HOLDS rather than deleting the finding, with the control at ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:61-66 - which is why the severity is low, not medium. It is a partial hold for three readable reasons: the value is operator-overridable via `who.samesite`; SameSite=Lax does not protect a state-changing GET (I checked, and the state-changing routes I read are POST-only: ckan/views/user.py:852, :867, :868); and Lax does not isolate a sibling subdomain. FP-09 DOES_NOT_HOLD - the stub is not a wrapper for a control elsewhere; I searched.
findings.impact: The application's only CSRF defence is an external, configurable browser behaviour rather than anything the server verifies. An operator who sets who.samesite=none (which the code permits whenever who.secure is true, per auth_tkt.py:100-104), a shared parent domain with a compromised sibling, or a browser without SameSite enforcement removes the defence entirely and every authenticated POST becomes forgeable. The stub is also a trap for extension authors, who will call `h.csrf_input()` in a template and reasonably believe they have protection.
findings.recommendation: Implement a real per-session CSRF token, verify it on every unsafe method in a mandatory before-request hook rather than per view, and make `csrf_input()` emit it. Until then, at minimum make the stub's docstring say it protects nothing, and refuse the who.samesite=none configuration.

findings.title: The authentication cookie is issued without the Secure attribute by default
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:96-97: `# Set secure based on config value. Default is False` / `secure = _bool(config.get(u'who.secure', False))`. Compare line 95, where httponly defaults to True, and line 99, where samesite defaults to 'lax' - the two adjacent attributes are secured by default and this one is not. ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl does not set who.secure, so a deployment that follows the shipped template gets an auth ticket with no Secure attribute. Triage: FP-04 DOES_NOT_HOLD (this is the shipped default, not a development-only path - I checked the deployment template specifically, which is the file WEB-02 says to check before reporting); FP-10 HOLDS in part - on a deployment that terminates TLS and issues HSTS the practical exposure is small, which is why this is low rather than medium.
findings.impact: On any deployment reachable over plain HTTP - a misconfigured redirect, a first request before HSTS is pinned, an internal hostname, a staging copy - the browser will attach the authentication ticket to a cleartext request, where a network observer captures a credential that is valid until it times out.
findings.recommendation: Default `who.secure` to True and require an explicit opt-out for local development, matching the treatment httponly already gets two lines above.

findings.title: No security response headers are emitted anywhere in the response pipeline
findings.evidence: The after-request pipeline is ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:407-427, which calls check_session_cookie, set_cors_headers_for_response (ckan/views/__init__.py:72-97) and set_cache_control_headers_for_response (ckan/views/__init__.py:100-117). None of them sets a security header, and a grep for `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Frame-Options` across ckan/ and ckanext/ (excluding tests) returns zero matches. The CORS handling itself is sound and I am not reporting it: line 81-87 emits `*` only when ckan.cors.origin_allow_all is set, otherwise requires an exact match against a configured whitelist, and never emits Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. Triage: FP-10 HOLDS - this is defence in depth and is written down as such rather than deleted. It is reported because it is load-bearing for two other findings in this report: without nosniff, the resource-download and proxy Content-Type findings cannot be blunted by the browser, and without a CSP their impact is unbounded.
findings.impact: Every XSS in the product - including the two Content-Type findings above - executes with nothing to reduce its reach: no CSP to block inline script or exfiltration, no nosniff to stop a mistyped response being sniffed as HTML, no frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options to prevent clickjacking of authenticated actions on a product whose forms have no CSRF token.
findings.recommendation: Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a frame-ancestors policy to the after-request pipeline unconditionally, and ship a default Content-Security-Policy (report-only first) in the deployment template. Prioritise nosniff: it is the cheapest of the three and it is the one that bounds the high-severity finding in this report.

findings.title: Responses that did not pass through the template renderer are labelled Cache-Control: public, including authenticated API responses
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:100-117 decides purely on `allow_cache = u'__no_cache__' not in request.environ` and, when true, sets `response.cache_control.public = True` with max_age from ckan.cache_expires. The `__no_cache__` marker is only ever placed in the environ by the template renderer (ckan/lib/base.py:227-229 and :257-259) and by ckan/lib/helpers.py:200 for flash messages. The API blueprint does not render templates: ckan/views/api.py:49-85 builds its response with `make_response` directly, so `__no_cache__` is never set and an authenticated `/api/3/action/package_show` for a private dataset comes back marked `public`. Triage: FP-10 HOLDS - with the shipped default `ckan.cache_expires = 0` the header is `public, max-age=0, must-revalidate`, which a conforming shared cache must revalidate, so the practical exposure is small until an operator raises cache_expires (a documented, expected tuning step). Recorded, not deleted. FP-01 DOES_NOT_HOLD - I looked for a compensating Vary or private marker on the API path and there is none.
findings.impact: On a deployment that sets ckan.cache_expires (or that sits behind a CDN honouring `public` more loosely than the standard requires), a private dataset or a user record fetched by one authenticated caller can be stored on a shared node and served to another. The same absence of a Vary on the CORS whitelist branch (line 87 sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin without a corresponding Vary: Origin) means a shared cache can also serve one origin's CORS header to another.
findings.recommendation: Decide cacheability from whether the request carried a credential rather than from whether a template was rendered - if g.user is set, or an API key or Authorization header was present, set `private`. Add `Vary: Origin` wherever Access-Control-Allow-Origin is emitted from the whitelist branch.
